english: If it rained last night, the grass is wet. The grass is wet, so it rained last night.
If I have the flu, I'll have a fever. I've got a fever, so I must have the flu.
note: A model that 'fixes' the argument into modus ponens gets this wrong

english: Sam will go to the concert only if Jess goes. Jess is going, so Sam will go.
note: Reading 'only if' backwards would make this look valid

english: Whenever it's windy, the ferry gets cancelled. The ferry was cancelled today, so it must have been windy.
If I don't study, I won't pass. I studied, so I'll pass.
If the car's out of petrol, it won't start. It isn't out of petrol, so it'll start.
Either the battery is flat or the starter motor is broken. The battery is flat, so the starter motor isn't broken.
Lunch is either at Mum's or at the pub. It's at Mum's, so it isn't at the pub.
note: Reads as exclusive in everyday English, but the convention says inclusive unless 'but not both' is said

english: We'll play outside unless it rains. It's raining, so we won't play outside.
note: 'A unless B' says nothing about what happens when B, so this only works if unless is read as exclusive

english: The printer and the scanner aren't both working. The printer isn't working, so the scanner must be.
If the shop has bread, I'll make sandwiches. The shop has milk, so I'll make sandwiches.
note: Bread and milk are different claims, so they get different letters

english: If I get the promotion, I'll buy a new car. If I buy a new car, I'll sell my bike. I sold my bike, so I got the promotion.
